name: Recruitment Channel Diversification
consequences: Increasing recruitment channels will raise enrollment speed, potentially exceeding the 30–35 participant target in year two, but may dilute pre‑screening quality, increasing the proportion of unproductive admissions and necessitating stricter exclusion verification.
options: Expand recruitment to include online sleep disorder forums and targeted social media ads to reach patients beyond local referrals.
Partner with regional sleep clinics to co-host educational webinars, positioning the unit as a trusted referral destination.
Implement a patient ambassador program where enrolled participants share experiences with peers, creating organic word‑of‑mouth referrals.
review: Broadening recruitment channels can accelerate enrollment but risks admitting participants who fail to meet strict inclusion criteria, potentially inflating the 20% unproductive admission threshold and triggering a costly external review.

name: Staffing Shift Rotation
consequences: A rotating shift model increases staff flexibility and reduces overtime, potentially lowering personnel costs, but may introduce variability in annotation consistency and increase training overhead for technicians transitioning between PSG and headband modalities.
options: Adopt a 12‑hour rotating shift schedule for technicians, ensuring continuous coverage while reducing overtime costs.
Introduce cross‑training for technicians in both PSG and headband monitoring to increase flexibility during peak event‑response periods.
Implement a staggered weekend rotation that pairs senior technicians with junior staff, fostering mentorship while maintaining night‑shift coverage.
review: Rotating shifts can cut overtime but may compromise annotation quality if technicians lack consistent exposure to the same monitoring modality, potentially inflating inter‑rater variability and delaying data processing.

name: Annotation Workflow Optimization
consequences: Optimizing annotation workflow can cut per‑event review time, accelerating data availability for analysis, but may increase reliance on technician judgment for initial markings, potentially raising inter‑rater variability if the triage criteria are not rigorously defined.
options: Deploy a real‑time annotation dashboard that flags potential events for technician triage, reducing manual review time.
Introduce a two‑tier annotation protocol where technicians first mark events, then senior reviewers confirm, streamlining workload distribution.
Integrate automated event‑detection scripts that pre‑label likely parasomnia episodes, allowing technicians to focus on verification rather than initial marking.
review: Streamlining annotation speeds up data processing but risks higher inter‑rater variability if technicians lack clear triage guidelines, potentially compromising the reliability of event counts used in phenotyping analyses.

name: Event‑Triage Algorithm Development
consequences: Developing an event‑triage algorithm can reduce manual review load, enabling faster data turnaround, but may introduce false positives that inflate annotation time and risk misclassifying benign movements as parasomnia, affecting downstream phenotyping accuracy.
options: Train a supervised machine‑learning model on annotated PSG data to predict parasomnia events from headband and sensor streams.
Leverage unsupervised clustering of multimodal sensor features to identify novel event signatures, reducing reliance on labeled data.
Implement a hybrid rule‑based filter that flags high‑probability events for human review, balancing automation with expert oversight.
review: An automated triage system cuts review time but may generate false positives, increasing technician workload and potentially skewing event frequency estimates if benign movements are misclassified as parasomnia.

name: Compensation Structure
consequences: Adjusting compensation can improve participant retention and event yield, but higher payouts increase budget strain and may attract individuals motivated by financial gain rather than clinical relevance, potentially biasing the sample.
options: Introduce a tiered compensation model that rewards longer stays with incremental bonuses, incentivizing participants to remain until multiple events are captured.
Offer flexible meal plans and local transport vouchers to reduce participant burden, potentially improving retention and data completeness.
Implement a pre‑admission credit system where participants receive a refundable deposit that is returned upon study completion, enhancing commitment.
review: Higher compensation may boost enrollment and event capture but risks inflating costs and attracting participants whose primary motivation is financial, potentially compromising the representativeness of the study cohort.

name: Expansion Timing Decision
consequences: Choosing expansion timing balances resource allocation against data quality; early expansion may strain staffing and increase false‑alarm rates, while delayed expansion preserves quality but limits participant throughput and delays publication timelines.
options: Delay suite expansion until the pilot cohort demonstrates a false‑alarm rate below 5%, ensuring data quality before scaling capacity.
Proceed with a phased expansion to 12 suites after achieving a 90% event‑capture success rate in the first 20 participants.
Implement a real‑time monitoring dashboard that flags capacity bottlenecks, allowing dynamic adjustment of suite utilization without full physical expansion.
review: Expanding suites early can boost enrollment but risks compromising data integrity if staffing and annotation pipelines are not fully mature, potentially leading to higher false‑alarm rates and delayed analyses.

name: Participant Retention Incentive Design
consequences: Adjusting the incentive structure can improve participant retention, potentially extending stay durations and data yield, but it also raises per-participant costs and may introduce bias if participants alter reporting to maximize compensation.
options: Offer tiered cash compensation tied to total nights, incentivizing longer stays but increasing per-participant cost.
Provide complimentary health consultations and sleep hygiene workshops, reducing monetary expense while fostering participant engagement.
Introduce a points-based reward system redeemable for local cultural experiences, engaging participants without direct cash outlay but requiring coordination with local partners.
review: While tiered cash compensation may boost retention, it risks inflating budget and could bias self-reporting of symptoms; non-monetary perks may not be equally motivating across demographics; the points system adds logistical complexity and may dilute focus on scientific outcomes.

name: Suite Utilization Scheduling
consequences: Reconfiguring suite scheduling can maximize occupancy and reduce idle time, yet it may limit the ability to rapidly respond to unexpected parasomnia events, potentially missing critical data.
options: Implement fixed nightly block scheduling, maximizing suite occupancy but limiting rapid response to flagged events.
Adopt a staggered shift model with overlapping nights, increasing responsiveness but complicating staffing coordination.
Introduce a dynamic booking algorithm that reallocates suites based on real-time event likelihood, optimizing utilization but requiring sophisticated monitoring.
review: Fixed nightly blocks streamline operations but may delay capture of sporadic events; staggered shifts enhance responsiveness yet strain staffing; dynamic allocation optimizes use but adds algorithmic complexity and potential scheduling conflicts.

name: Data Annotation Workflow Automation
consequences: Automating annotation reduces manual labor and speeds data processing, but reliance on imperfect algorithms can introduce systematic errors that compromise event validity and downstream analyses.
options: Deploy semi-automated event detection using machine learning to pre-label events, reducing scorer time but requiring periodic human review.
Introduce rule-based threshold alerts for abnormal sensor patterns, speeding annotation but risking false positives.
Implement a hybrid crowdsourcing platform where trained volunteers assist in preliminary labeling, lowering costs but raising consistency concerns.
review: Semi-automated detection cuts scorer workload but depends on model accuracy; rule-based alerts may flood with false positives, burdening reviewers; volunteer crowdsourcing reduces cost yet may compromise labeling quality and data integrity.

name: Ethics Compliance Cadence
consequences: Altering the frequency of ethics reviews can accelerate protocol changes and recruitment, yet it may overwhelm oversight bodies and increase administrative burden, potentially compromising thoroughness.
options: Adopt quarterly ethics board reviews to accelerate protocol adjustments, expediting recruitment but increasing administrative load.
Maintain annual reviews to ensure thorough oversight, slowing changes but providing stability.
Implement a rolling review process with continuous monitoring, balancing agility and oversight but requiring additional compliance staff.
review: Quarterly reviews accelerate protocol changes but may overwhelm the board and staff; annual reviews offer stability but can delay necessary adaptations; rolling reviews provide balance yet demand extra compliance resources and may dilute board focus.

name: Funding Allocation Flexibility
consequences: Shifting budget allocations across years can provide resources for emergent needs, but it risks misaligning spending with milestone-driven deliverables and eroding contingency reserves.
options: Reallocate unused year-one funds to year-two equipment upgrades, accelerating capability but reducing contingency for unforeseen costs.
Maintain strict year-by-year budget lock, ensuring milestone alignment but limiting responsiveness to emerging needs.
Introduce a rolling reserve fund that can be tapped across years, providing flexibility but demanding rigorous monitoring.
review: Reallocating year-one funds accelerates upgrades but erodes safety net for later contingencies; strict yearly locks preserve milestone focus but hinder rapid response; a rolling reserve offers flexibility yet demands vigilant oversight to prevent misallocation.

name: Interdisciplinary Collaboration Structure
consequences: Redesigning collaboration mechanisms can enhance integration of clinical and technical expertise, yet it may create role ambiguity and increase coordination overhead, potentially slowing decision cycles.
options: Establish a joint steering committee with representatives from neurology, engineering, and psychology, fostering cross-disciplinary input but potentially slowing decision-making.
Create dedicated liaison roles that bridge clinical and technical teams, improving communication but adding personnel costs.
Implement a shared digital workspace for real-time data sharing and discussion, enhancing transparency but requiring secure infrastructure.
review: A joint steering committee promotes integration but may create decision bottlenecks; liaison roles improve communication yet increase staffing costs; a shared workspace boosts transparency but demands robust security and may expose sensitive data.

name: Participant Screening Efficiency
consequences: Accelerating the pre‑admission screening process shortens enrollment time but may increase the proportion of ineligible participants, potentially pushing the unproductive admission rate above the 20% threshold and delaying study milestones.
options: Deploy an online pre‑screening questionnaire that flags obvious exclusions before the clinic visit, reducing in‑person triage time.
Conduct a brief in‑person cognitive assessment to detect excessive sleepiness and rule out untreated sleep apnea early.
Collect a 7‑day sleep diary via mobile app prior to admission to refine eligibility and anticipate event likelihood.
review: Relying on an online questionnaire risks missing nuanced clinical exclusions that only a clinician can detect, potentially inflating the unproductive admission rate beyond the 20% threshold and delaying study milestones.

name: Night Shift Staffing Model
consequences: Shifting to a 12‑hour shift schedule reduces overtime costs but increases cumulative fatigue, potentially compromising safety during critical event escalations and raising the risk of missed or mis‑annotated episodes.
options: Adopt a 12‑hour shift schedule with staggered start times to reduce overtime costs.
Introduce a part‑time night technician pool to provide flexible coverage during peak event periods.
Implement a cross‑training program so technicians can cover both night and day duties, improving workforce resilience.
review: A 12‑hour shift may cut overtime but increases cumulative fatigue, potentially compromising safety during critical event escalations and raising the risk of missed or mis‑annotated episodes.

name: Data Storage Scalability
consequences: Expanding on‑premise storage capacity ensures data integrity but raises capital expenditure and may delay nightly encrypted backups, potentially impacting real‑time annotation workflows.
options: Upgrade NAS to a clustered RAID system with hot‑spare disks to handle peak data loads.
Offload raw sensor streams to a cloud storage tier with automated lifecycle policies to reduce on‑premise footprint.
Implement a tiered archival strategy, moving older nights to tape storage while keeping recent data on SSDs.
review: Moving data to cloud storage introduces latency in real‑time annotation and raises compliance concerns around cross‑border data transfer, potentially violating German data protection regulations.

name: Ethics Review Cadence
consequences: Consolidating ethics amendments speeds approvals but may overlook specific safety concerns, while a rapid sub‑committee may lack depth, potentially compromising ethical rigor.
options: Submit a consolidated ethics amendment covering all protocol changes to reduce review cycles.
Establish a standing ethics sub‑committee to provide rapid feedback on minor protocol adjustments.
Leverage the university's central ethics portal to track and automate submission status updates.
review: Consolidating all amendments risks overlooking specific participant safety concerns, while a rapid sub‑committee may lack the depth of a full board review, potentially compromising ethical rigor.

name: Control Group Matching Strategy
consequences: Recruiting matched controls improves baseline comparison but increases recruitment burden and cost, potentially stretching the 3‑year budget and delaying data collection.
options: Recruit controls from the same sleep clinic waiting list to ensure similar demographic profiles.
Use a community volunteer pool screened for normal sleep patterns to serve as controls.
Implement a virtual control cohort by re‑using anonymized data from prior studies with comparable protocols.
review: Relying on a virtual control cohort may introduce hidden selection bias, as anonymized data may lack contextual variables critical for accurate baseline comparison.

name: Event Annotation Workflow
consequences: Optimizing annotation reduces manual labor but may lower inter‑rater reliability if shortcuts are introduced, potentially compromising the validity of event adjudication.
options: Introduce a real‑time flagging system that highlights probable events for immediate technician review.
Use a semi‑automated scoring template that standardizes key metrics before final human adjudication.
Implement a peer‑review rotation where technicians cross‑check each other’s annotations nightly.
review: Adding a real‑time flagging system may overload technicians during peak event periods, leading to missed annotations and potentially lowering overall data quality.
